_comment: The ratio of valgebra to pydantic's strict TypeAdapter each shape must stay under: a claim the project makes, not a measurement it recorded. The argument for the ceilings, for the recorded block beside them and for the one shape excluded from it is docs/dev/07-tooling-ci.md, under 'The competitive ratio' -- a page the documentation lint reads and this file is not. Changing a ceiling or re-recording a ratio is an edit with an argument in its commit message; scripts/perf_gate.py --against is the fine-grained gate.
_free_threaded_comment: Ceilings the free-threaded build is held to instead, for the shapes where it is a different performance environment rather than the same one on a slower clock. A shape absent from here is held to the shared ceiling above. Reading an element out of a list takes the list's lock there, and a shape whose cost is per-element pays it; docs/11-performance.md measures that and says which shapes part. The bench lane's free-threaded job runs on two classes of machine, the faster about twice the speed of the slower, and on two shapes pydantic gains more from the faster one than the walk does: over the job's 304 readings from 2026-09-12 to 2026-10-09 the schema nested twenty-five deep read 0.291 to 0.453 and the one-integer check 0.171 to 0.305, each highest on the faster class, and two commits whose walk is the same read the nested schema 0.378 on the slower class and 0.449 on the faster. A ceiling inside that range fires on the runner rather than on the code, so each of the two clears the highest reading it has taken by a fifth, rounded up to the next 0.05.
_recorded_comment: The ratio each shape last measured, the spread it was measured across, and the environment both belong to. See docs/dev/07-tooling-ci.md for why a claim alone stopped being enough.

unratcheted.error_report: Not measurable on this instrument. Five runs of one PGO CPython 3.12 build read 0.861, 0.882, 0.889, 1.056 and 1.193 -- a spread of 0.33, a third of the shape's own value, where every other shape spreads between 0.001 and 0.048. Twelve runs of another PGO CPython 3.12 build read 0.43 to 0.46 (docs/11-performance.md), so the spread is the build's as much as the shape's. A tolerance wide enough not to fire on that noise would be wider than any regression worth catching, and a tighter one would fire constantly. The shape keeps its ceiling of 1.60, which it is nowhere near crossing, and the reason it is noisy is worth its own reading: it is the only shape timing a path that raises and formats an exception, so a Python exception's cost is inside the measurement.

recorded._how_recorded: Armed from a window of the bench lane's own readings, not from one run: the lane reads one tree on several classes of machine further apart than a tolerance, and a ratio recorded from one run fires on the next run that lands on another class. `window` holds the readings -- the comparison table each bench job printed on CPython 3.14 from run 38075383084 on 2026-10-10, the first after the walk context was cut to seven words (the nested schema read about 0.157 before it and 0.131 after), to run 38169864035 on 2026-10-11: eleven runs, on all three classes of runner the lane drew, a pydantic scalar taking about 160, 240 and 310 ns on them. Each ratio is the window's median. Each tolerance is half again the widest reading above the recorded median, in the window or in the lane's 53 readings of 2026-10-04 to 2026-10-10 before it, rounded up to a two-hundredth, and never below what the shape spreads on one box. The nested schema's is its own reading of 0.173 on run 38169864035, where the run before it, with the same walk and the same profile on the same class of runner, read 0.125: one tree lays that walk out differently from one profiled build to the next. large_array's carries one reading of 0.149, on a run whose next two read 0.118 and 0.127. The last two runs follow the profile's training of the JSON document, which reads about 0.58 after it against 0.66 before, so its floor is loose until a window read after the training records it again. A change that moves a shape on the lane is recorded again from readings taken after it, with --record-window.
